title: Toward a Perceptual Theory of Transparency

findings.antecedent: mean luminance within the matching disk (Lmean)
findings.consequent: luminance range set to match perceived transmittance (Lrange)
findings.mechanism: The visual system's computation of transmittance is influenced by the overall luminance context, leading to a higher luminance range setting for higher mean luminances to maintain perceived transmittance.
findings.quote: as the mean luminance within the matching disk increases, observers set a higher luminance range to match the perceived transmittance of a fixed target disk.

findings.consequent: slopes of linear fits for transmittance matches
findings.mechanism: The visual system's sensitivity to contrast influences how perceived transmittance scales with mean luminance.
findings.quote: as the contrast within the target disk increases, so do the slopes of these linear fits.

findings.consequent: perceived transmittance (as predicted by Metelli's model, Equation 10)
findings.mechanism: Metelli's model predicts that perceived transmittance should be independent of mean luminance, which is contradicted by empirical observations.
findings.quote: This solution predicts that the transmittance matches... should be independent of mean luminance.

findings.consequent: perceived transmittance (when replotted in Michelson contrast)
findings.mechanism: When data are transformed to Michelson contrast, the perceived transmittance becomes independent of mean luminance, suggesting Michelson contrast is the underlying variable.
findings.quote: each of the data curves becomes essentially independent of mean luminance.

findings.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast, not luminance range, as the critical variable for computing and assigning surface transmittance.
findings.quote: the critical variable that the visual system uses to assign surface transmittance is Michelson contrast, not luminance range.

findings.mechanism: Observers systematically overestimate the transmittance of darkening transparent surfaces.
findings.quote: Observers systematically overestimate the transmittance of darkening transparent surfaces

findings.mechanism: Observers systematically underestimate the transmittance of lightening transparent surfaces.
findings.quote: they systematically underestimate the transmittance of lightening transparent surfaces.

findings.antecedent: transparent surface changes mean luminance of underlying surface
findings.consequent: magnitude of over/underestimation of perceived transmittance
findings.mechanism: The perceived transmittance depends on the interaction between the transparent surface's attributes and those of the occluded surface.
findings.quote: the magnitude of this overestimation (or underestimation) of surface transmittance is directly proportional to the extent to which the transparent surface decreases (or increases) the mean luminance of the underlying surface.

findings.mechanism: Estimating lightness of a transparent surface involves more variables and is thus a more complex cognitive task.
findings.quote: Observers reported the lightness-matching task to be much less natural and substantially more difficult.

findings.mechanism: Increased task difficulty leads to more strategic influences and less consistent judgments.
findings.quote: the lightness matches exhibit a fair degree of variability across observers.

findings.mechanism: Metelli's model predicts a stronger convergence of lightness matches than observed, indicating an incomplete discounting of the underlying layer.
findings.source: Results and Discussion, Experiment 2; Figure 11, Table 2
findings.quote: the extent of this convergence is considerably weaker than predicted by the term T

findings.antecedent: observers' attempt to estimate lightness of transparent layer
findings.mechanism: Lightness judgments are biased towards the mean luminance of the transparent region, indicating incomplete discounting of the underlying surface.
findings.quote: their matches are biased strongly toward the mean luminance in the region of transparency.

findings.antecedent: Metelli's magnitude constraint (Condition 2: lower luminance difference)
findings.mechanism: Observers consistently failed to perceive transparency in conditions where luminance range was lowered but Michelson contrast was increased, contradicting Metelli's magnitude constraint.
findings.quote: observers do not perceive transparency in the regime R-C+ even though luminance range was lowered... thus providing a counter to Metelli's magnitude constraint.

findings.antecedent: transparent layers darken underlying surface (Lmean < Lo)
findings.consequent: ease and reliability of transparency judgments
findings.mechanism: An asymmetry exists in processing darkening vs. lightening transparent layers, possibly due to evolutionary mechanisms for shadows.
findings.quote: judgments of transparency are easy and reliable for darkening transparent layers

findings.antecedent: transparent layers lighten underlying surface (Lmean > Lo)
findings.consequent: ease and reliability of transparency judgments
findings.mechanism: An asymmetry exists in processing darkening vs. lightening transparent layers, possibly due to evolutionary mechanisms for shadows.
findings.quote: difficult and more variable for lightening layers.

findings.antecedent: Michelson contrast within central disk is lower than in surround
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast as a critical image variable to initiate perceptual scission and transparency.
findings.quote: observers see transparency when the Michelson contrast within the central disk is lower than in the surround

stimuli.description: Large circular disk with vertically oriented sinusoidal grating (background) and a smaller disk placed inside (target disk) with lower contrast. Disparity was introduced to the boundary of the small disk to create a percept of a transparent filter floating in front of the grating. Luminance range and mean luminance were varied across experiments.

limitations: The study primarily focused on models of transparency that involve only light-transmitting properties, ignoring light-scattering properties of translucent media. Therefore, the findings may not fully generalize to translucent surfaces where blur is an additional cue for opacity.

The lightness-matching task was reported as considerably more difficult and variable, suggesting it is more prone to strategic influences, which might affect the generalizability of these specific lightness findings.
